summary: Specifies how Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 are used when Proxy Mobile IPv6 manages mobility, including for mobile nodes that do not take part in mobility signaling. It aims to reduce handover delay and packet loss. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: When a phone moves from one tower to the next, the network gets ready ahead of time so the call doesn't drop.

questions: what is proxy mobile ipv6 fast handover
what is a pmag and nmag
what is the f flag in handover initiate
subtitle: How a mobile device can move between access routers without dropping packets, even when the device itself takes no part in the signaling.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 lets the network handle mobility for devices that know nothing about it, but its handover delay and packet loss are no better than plain Mobile IPv6. Fast handovers for Mobile IPv6 assume the mobile node sends the signaling itself.
tldr.mechanism: The two gateways involved, the previous and the new Mobile Access Gateway, talk to each other using extended Handover Initiate and Handover Acknowledge messages. They transfer the mobile node's context and set up a tunnel so packets keep flowing during the move.
tldr.outcome: The mobile node needs no changes and the Local Mobility Anchor needs no new functions. The protocol is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5949 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Proxy Mobile IPv6 Needs Fast Handovers
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6, RFC 5213) gives IP mobility to a mobile node that does not support Mobile IPv6. A proxy agent in the network does the mobility signaling on the node's behalf. The catch, according to the RFC, is that PMIPv6 handover latency and packet loss are considered no different from those of Mobile IPv6.

Fast handovers for Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6, RFC 5568) cut that delay, but they depend on the mobile node sending messages such as Fast Binding Update. This document extends FMIPv6 for PMIPv6 so that handover delay and packet loss are minimized and network-resident context can be transferred during a PMIPv6 handover. RFC 5568 stays normative except where this document specifies new or revised functions and messages.
sections.eli5: Normally the phone has to shout out that it is moving. Here the network does the talking for the phone, so the phone does not need to know anything special.

sections.title: The Players and the Reference Network
sections.content:
PMIPv6 has two core entities. The Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) is the topological anchor point for the mobile node's home network prefix and tracks its binding state. The Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) acts as the access router for the mobile node, detects its movements and registers it with the LMA. In this document the MAG and the access router are co-located, so the Previous Access Router (PAR) and New Access Router (NAR) are interchangeable with the PMAG and NMAG.

The access networks (P-AN before the move, N-AN after) are made of access points, often called base stations in cellular networks. A handover indication is a generic message from the P-AN to the PMAG saying that a mobile node is moving. Its details depend on the access technology and are outside the scope of the RFC.

Because the mobile node takes no part in IP mobility signaling, the FMIPv6 messages that involve it (RtSolPr, PrRtAdv, FBU, FBack and UNA) are not applicable. A MAG that receives a RtSolPr or FBU from a mobile node SHOULD either behave as if it does not implement FMIPv6, or start serving that node as RFC 5568 specifies. The protocol is transparent to the LMA, so there is no new functional requirement on it.
sections.eli5: Think of two bus stops with a dispatcher at each. The dispatchers, not the passenger, arrange the handoff when the passenger walks from one stop to the other.

sections.title: Predictive and Reactive Handover
sections.content:
FMIPv6 has two modes. In the predictive mode, a bidirectional tunnel between the PMAG and NMAG is established before the mobile node attaches to the NMAG. In the reactive mode, the tunnel is set up after the node attaches. All MAGs are REQUIRED to have the capability and resources to buffer packets for the mobile nodes they serve.

In the predictive flow, the mobile node reports a likely new access point, the P-AN sends a handover indication to the PMAG, and the PMAG derives the NMAG from the new access point identifier. The PMAG sends a Handover Initiate (HI) message with the P flag set, carrying the mobile node identifier, its home network prefix(es) and the address of its LMA. The NMAG answers with a Handover Acknowledge (HAck), also with P set. Later the NMAG sends the Proxy Binding Update to the LMA and receives the Proxy Binding Acknowledgment; the RFC notes those two steps are not part of the fast handover itself.

In the reactive flow, the NMAG sends the HI to the PMAG after the mobile node has attached. The HI MUST have the P flag set and include the mobile node identifier, and MAY include a Context Request option. The PMAG replies with the home network prefix(es) or IPv4 home address and, if the context cannot be supplied, returns Code 131. If the NMAG asked for forwarding and the PMAG cannot do it, the PMAG returns Code 132. How the NMAG finds the PMAG is not specified.

The timing of context transfer and of packet forwarding can differ. The U flag asks for buffering and the new F flag asks for forwarding, so an HI with U set can be sent earlier than the one with F set. When forwarding is complete, the PMAG MAY send an HI with F set and Code 2 so both ends can tear down the tunnel together.
sections.eli5: Predictive is like the old bus stop calling the new one before you walk over. Reactive is the new stop calling the old one after you have already arrived. Either way, your bag is passed along so nothing gets lost.

sections.title: The Tunnel Between Gateways
sections.content:
When a MAG receives an HI with the F flag set, it prepares to send and receive the mobile node's packets to and from the other MAG and returns a HAck with the same sequence number. Both MAGs SHOULD support these encapsulation modes, which are also used between the LMA and MAG:

  • IPv4-or-IPv6-over-IPv6, IPv4-or-IPv6-over-IPv4 and IPv4-or-IPv6-over-IPv4-UDP (RFC 5844)
  • TLV-header UDP tunneling (RFC 5845)
  • GRE tunneling with or without GRE keys (RFC 5845)

The two MAGs MUST use the same mechanism. The RECOMMENDED default is the same encapsulation as the LMA-to-MAG tunnel, which needs no extra configuration. It can be overridden by configuration or by a negotiation mechanism that is outside the scope of the document. With GRE keys, the NMAG picks the key for downlink packets and the PMAG picks the key for uplink packets, and they are exchanged in the GRE Key option.

Downlink packets from the LMA go to the PMAG, which tunnels them to the NMAG. The NMAG SHOULD send them on to the N-AN right away if the node is ready, otherwise it SHOULD buffer them. Uplink packets are reverse-tunneled from the NMAG to the PMAG, which sends them to the LMA. In PMIPv6 the mobile node uses only its home address, so the PMAG forwards to the NMAG rather than to a new care-of address, and the NMAG can create a neighbor cache entry and routes from the context it received before the node even performs Neighbor Discovery.

If a MAG hits an error such as insufficient buffer space, it SHOULD immediately send a HAck with the cause and cancel all tunneling operations. For IPv4, the IPv4 Address option carries the IPv4 home address and the LMA Address option carries the IPv4 address of the LMA.
sections.eli5: The two gateways dig a private tunnel between them. Your packets slide through it to the new place while you are still switching over.

sections.title: The HI and HAck Messages
sections.content:
This RFC extends two Mobility Header messages from RFC 5568. In both, the P flag (Proxy flag) distinguishes the new format from the original and MUST be set in all new message formats defined here. The F flag (Forwarding flag) requests forwarding of the mobile node's packets. The S flag MUST be zero in this specification. The mobile node identifier MUST be present, so the target node is uniquely identified, and each message carries context for exactly one mobile node.

For the HI message, with P set, the Code field is zero by default, or 2 (completion of forwarding) or 3 (all available context transferred). For the HAck message, Code 0 means handover accepted or successful, 5 means context transfer accepted, 6 means all available context transferred, and 128 to 130 are reused from RFC 5568. Two codes are new: 131 (requested context not available) and 132 (forwarding not available).

In the predictive mode the NMAG answers a context-carrying HI with Code 5. In the reactive mode the PMAG answers with Code 6 if all available context fits, or Code 5 if more is available, in which case the NMAG MAY send further HI messages for the rest. Code 131 is returned, with no context, if none of the requested context is available.
sections.eli5: The messages are like notes passed between the gateways. A little flag says "this is the proxy kind of note", and a number says how it went, such as "OK" or "I cannot do that".

sections.title: Mobility Options for Moving Context
sections.content:
The context moves in mobility options. Three are new: the Context Request option (type 40), the Local Mobility Anchor Address option (type 41) and the Mobile Node Link-Local Address Interface Identifier option (type 42). The rest are reused from other RFCs.

  • Context Request is sent in an HI to ask for context. Its default request is the Home Network Prefix option, and the Mobile Node Link-layer Identifier option MUST also be requested if a link layer is available and used.
  • LMA Address carries the LMA's IPv6 address (Option-Code 1) or IPv4 address (Option-Code 2).
  • MN LLA-IID carries the interface identifier of the node's link-local address in the P-AN.
  • Home Network Prefix and Link-Local Address options are defined in RFC 5213.
  • The GRE Key option follows RFC 5845, the IPv4 Address option follows RFC 5844, and the Vendor-Specific option follows RFC 5094.

The NMAG can also use the prefix it learned to send a Router Advertisement as soon as the node attaches. If the HAck returns a different prefix or the later binding registration fails, the NMAG MUST withdraw the advertised prefix with another Router Advertisement carrying zero prefix lifetime.
sections.eli5: The options are the items packed in the bag that gets handed over: your address, your ID and where your home base is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security follows RFC 5213 and RFC 5568. The MAG and LMA are assumed to share security associations, and so are the PMAG and NMAG.

HI and HAck messages MUST be protected with end-to-end security associations offering integrity and data origin authentication, and both gateways MUST implement IPsec (RFC 4301). IPsec ESP in transport mode with integrity protection SHOULD be used for this signaling, and confidentiality SHOULD be added when sensitive context about the mobile node is transferred. ESP in tunnel mode SHOULD protect the mobile node's forwarded packets if the PMAG-to-NMAG link exposes them to more threats than their normal routed path.
sections.eli5: The gateways must lock their notes in an envelope so nobody can read or fake them while they travel.
